$comment: Chapter prose for ch00 to ch02 (content builder), ICU MessageFormat. Placeholders are filled from data/constants.json through each content.json, so no measured number is written here. No scripture wording belongs in this file: verses come from data/quran.json, and hadith wording only from reviewed entries in data/hadith.json. Hadith summaries are indirect speech, never quotations; the panel shows each under the label ui.hadith.summaryLabel and says separately when the verified wording is still pending. Tafsir summaries await scholarly review (docs/SPEC.md section 9).
ch00.intro.title: Before creation
ch00.intro.subtitle: Stillness, and a single word of command
ch00.caption.word: The Quran speaks of creation coming to be through a single word of command.
ch00.caption.beyond: Whether anything came before the beginning of time lies beyond what physics can test.
ch00.text.kunNote: The single word shown in calligraphy in this chapter is taken from the Tanzil text of this verse and set in the Amiri Quran typeface.
ch00.hadith.bukhari3191.summary: In this hadith the Prophet ﷺ speaks of Allah (glorified and exalted is He) existing when nothing else existed, of His Throne being over the water, of His writing all things in the Dhikr, and of His creating the heavens and the earth.
ch00.hadith.muslim2653.summary: In this hadith the Prophet ﷺ tells that the measures of creation were written fifty thousand years before the heavens and the earth were created, while His Throne was over the water.
ch00.hadith.pen.summary: In this hadith the Prophet ﷺ tells that the first thing Allah created was the Pen, and that it was commanded to write.
ch00.hadith.abudawud4700.note: This narration and Jami at-Tirmidhi 2155 are together known as the hadith of the Pen. Al-Albani graded this narration sahih; at-Tirmidhi notes that his narration is gharib by its chain. Both gradings are shown.
ch00.hadith.tirmidhi2155.note: The same hadith of the Pen as Sunan Abi Dawud 4700, reported through a different chain.
ch00.scholarly.classical.originator: On 2:117, Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is called the Originator of the heavens and the earth because He created them when nothing like them had existed before. He quotes al-Tabari’s commentary to the same effect, that they were brought into being without any precedent, and calls that explanation sound.
ch00.scholarly.classical.command: On the command in 2:117 and 36:82, Ibn Kathir explains that it shows the completeness of His power and authority: what He wills comes to be by His command alone, and a single command suffices, needing no repetition or confirmation.
ch00.scholarly.classical.pen: A hadith states the first thing Allah created was the Pen, commanded to write. Many scholars, including Ibn Hajar, understood this to mean first after the Throne and the water, or first in the command to write, since other authentic hadith mention the Throne already over the water.
ch00.science.limits: Physics has no tested description of what, if anything, came before the beginning of cosmic time. Our best-tested theories trace the history of the universe back about {age} billion years, to a hot, dense state.
ch00.science.theories: Closer still to the first instant, general relativity is expected to break down, and a tested theory of quantum gravity does not yet exist. In general relativity, time is part of the universe being described, not a stage set apart from it.
ch00.open.beginningOfTime: Did time itself have a beginning, or does the earliest moment we can describe mark only the edge of our present theories?
ch00.open.before: Some proposals describe a phase before the hot Big Bang, such as eternal inflation or a bounce from an earlier contracting universe. None has been confirmed by observation.
ch01.intro.title: The beginning
ch01.intro.subtitle: A hot, dense beginning, and space itself stretching
ch01.caption.beginning: Our universe can be traced back to a beginning that was hot and dense beyond imagining.
ch01.caption.stretch: Space itself stretches, carrying everything within it.
ch01.caption.cooling: As space expanded, the young universe cooled.
ch01.caption.sideBySide: The verse and the science are placed side by side for reflection, not as proof of one another.
ch01.caption.open: How the beginning itself came to be remains one of the deepest open questions in science.
ch01.scholarly.classical.joined: In his commentary on 21:30, Ibn Kathir explains that in the beginning the heavens and the earth were joined together, one upon another, and that Allah (glorified and exalted is He) then separated them, made the heavens seven and the earth seven, and placed the air between the earth and the lowest heaven. He cites Sa’id ibn Jubayr, that the earth became separate when the sky was raised, and al-Hasan and Qatadah, that the two were separated by the air between them.
ch01.scholarly.classical.rain: Ibn Kathir also records another early report, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): the sky was closed and gave no rain, and the earth was closed and grew no plants, until both were opened, the sky with rain and the earth with vegetation.
ch01.scholarly.modern.bigBang: Some modern writers read this as resembling the Big Bang. This is a modern reading, not the classical one.
ch01.science.age: The universe is {age} billion years old, with an uncertainty of {ageErr} million years. This figure comes from the Planck satellite’s measurements of the cosmic microwave background, combined with the gravitational lensing of that radiation and with galaxy-clustering data, and it assumes the standard ΛCDM model of cosmology.
ch01.science.hotDense: Several independent lines of evidence point to a hot, dense early universe: the expansion of space, the abundances of the lightest elements, and the cosmic microwave background, an almost perfect thermal glow that has cooled to {cmbT} kelvin today.
ch01.science.expansion: The Big Bang was not an explosion into empty space. Space itself has been expanding everywhere, carrying distant galaxies apart and stretching their light to longer wavelengths.
ch01.science.inflation: Cosmic inflation proposes a brief burst of extremely rapid expansion in the first instant. It would explain why the universe looks so uniform on large scales and where its first tiny ripples came from. It fits the microwave background well and is well supported, but it has not been directly confirmed.
ch01.open.firstInstant: What happened at the very first instant, where today’s physics breaks down?
ch01.open.inflation: Did inflation happen, and if so, what drove it? Primordial gravitational waves imprinted on the microwave background would be strong evidence; none has been detected so far.
ch02.intro.title: The first light
ch02.intro.subtitle: From glowing plasma to the oldest light we can see
ch02.caption.nuclei: In its first few minutes, the universe forged helium and traces of other light nuclei from protons and neutrons.
ch02.caption.opaque: For a long age afterwards, light could not travel freely through the hot, glowing plasma.
ch02.caption.atoms: As it cooled, electrons joined nuclei to form the first atoms, and the universe became transparent.
ch02.caption.planck: That light still reaches us, stretched into microwaves. This is the real sky map of it from ESA’s Planck satellite.
ch02.caption.seeds: Its faint variations in temperature trace the seeds from which galaxies would later grow.
ch02.text.smokeNote: This chapter does not identify the smoke in this verse with the glowing plasma of the early universe or with the microwave background shown in the scene.
ch02.scholarly.classical.smoke: Classical commentators describe the smoke (dukhan) in this verse as steam or vapour. Ibn Kathir, commenting on 41:11, explains it as steam that rose up when the earth was created.
ch02.scholarly.classical.order: The commentators also note that in these verses the earth’s creation is mentioned before the heavens were shaped. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah (glorified and exalted is He) created the earth first because it is the foundation, laid before the roof. He reconciles this with 79:30 through a reply of Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), recorded by al-Bukhari: the earth itself was created first, and its spreading out came after the heavens were made.
ch02.science.bbn: In its first few minutes, the universe forged the lightest nuclei. Ordinary matter emerged as about {hMass}% hydrogen and {heMass} ± {heMassErr}% helium by mass, or roughly {hNum}% hydrogen and {heNum}% helium by number of atoms.
ch02.science.traces: Small traces of other light nuclei formed too: {d} ± {dErr} deuterium atoms for every million hydrogen atoms, a little helium-3, and a little lithium-7. The oldest stars show {li} ± {liErr} lithium-7 atoms for every ten billion hydrogen atoms, though they may have destroyed some of their own lithium.
ch02.science.recombination: For about {recAge} years the universe was filled with a hot, opaque plasma in which light could not travel far. Once it had cooled to about {recT} kelvin, electrons and nuclei combined into neutral atoms and light was set free. This last scattering of light happened at a redshift of about {z}.
ch02.science.cmb: That light, stretched by the expansion of space, reaches us today as the cosmic microwave background, with a temperature of {cmbT} ± {cmbTErr} kelvin. The map shows the Planck satellite’s measurement of its tiny temperature differences across the whole sky.
ch02.open.lithium: The cosmological lithium problem: the standard theory of Big Bang nucleosynthesis gives {liTheory} ± {liTheoryErr} lithium-7 atoms for every ten billion hydrogen atoms, about {factor} times more than old stars show ({li} ± {liErr}). Whether the cause lies in how stars destroy lithium, in nuclear data, or in new physics is unresolved.
ch02.open.helium3: The primordial amount of helium-3 is still poorly known: it can be measured only in the Solar System and in gas within our own Galaxy, both long since processed by stars.
ch03.intro.title: The dark ages and the first stars
ch03.intro.subtitle: Out of darkness, a web of unseen matter and the first starlight
ch03.note.text: No verse is placed beside this chapter. The science stands here on its own, between the passages before it and after it.
ch03.note.scholarly: With no verse in this chapter, there is no scholarly reading to summarise.
ch03.science.dark: After the first light was set free, no stars yet shone. For millions of years the universe was dark: astronomers call this time the cosmic dark ages.
ch03.science.web: Dark matter, which gives off no light but makes up most of the matter in the universe, drew together under its own gravity. The tiny differences in density seen in the cosmic microwave background grew into a vast web of sheets, filaments and knots.
ch03.science.method: The web on screen grows by the Zel’dovich approximation, a standard first approximation to how gravity amplifies those first ripples; full simulations follow the collapse further. Dark matter itself is invisible, so it is drawn here in false colour.
ch03.science.firstStars: The first stars probably formed in the densest knots, between about {earliest} and {latest} million years after the beginning (from a redshift of about {z} onward, in current models). They were made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium.
ch03.science.jwst: The James Webb Space Telescope has confirmed galaxies shining remarkably early. MoM-z14, at redshift {momZ}, is seen as it was about {momAge} million years after the beginning. JADES-GS-z14-0 was first measured at redshift {jadesNir} from its JWST spectrum, and ALMA has since pinned it to {jadesAlma}: about {jadesAge} million years after the beginning.
ch03.open.bright: Why are these early galaxies brighter, and why did they appear sooner, than many models expected? It is an open question.
ch03.open.popIII: No first-generation star has yet been seen directly.
ch03.caption.dark: After the first light, the universe went dark.
ch03.caption.web: Unseen matter gathered into a vast web.
ch03.caption.method: Shown in false colour: dark matter itself gives off no light.
ch03.caption.stars: In its densest knots, the first stars began to shine.
ch03.caption.webb: Telescopes today see galaxies from this early age, brighter than many expected.
ch03.caption.galaxies: Around the first stars, the first galaxies began to grow.
ch03.caption.open: How the first galaxies formed so quickly remains an open question.
ch04.intro.title: A vast heaven
ch04.intro.subtitle: Space itself grows, and the light crossing it stretches
ch04.scholarly.classical.vast: Ibn Kathir explains bi-aydin (literally “with hands”) as “with strength”, following Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Thawri and others. On la-musi‘un he says that Allah (glorified and exalted is He) made the sky vast and raised it high without pillars, so that it stands on its own.
ch04.scholarly.classical.capable: Al-Qurtubi records further readings: “We are capable” (Ibn Abbas) and “We are able” (al-Hasan); that Allah widens provision for His creation, through rain (al-Hasan); and “rich and capable”. He concludes that all of these fall within the verse’s meaning.
ch04.scholarly.modern.expanding: Some modern writers read la-musi‘un as “We are expanding it” and relate it to the expansion of the universe. This is a modern reading, not how the classical commentators explained the verse.
ch04.science.hubble: In 1929 Edwin Hubble showed that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it moves away from us: the universe is expanding.
ch04.science.redshift: Galaxies are not flying apart through space; the space between them is growing. Light crossing that growing space is stretched to longer, redder wavelengths. This is its redshift.
ch04.science.accelerating: In 1998 two teams studying distant exploding stars found that the expansion is speeding up.
ch04.science.tension: Measurements disagree on how fast the universe is expanding today. Inferences from the early universe give {planck} kilometres per second per megaparsec (Planck) to {act} (ACT with Planck and DESI), while nearby stars and supernovae (SH0ES) give {shoes}. This “Hubble tension” is unresolved.
ch04.science.darkEnergy: A cosmological constant is the simplest explanation for the speeding up. But DESI’s 2025 results, combined with the microwave background and supernovae, prefer a dark energy that weakens over time, at {min} to {max} sigma depending on the supernova sample: a hint, not yet a discovery.
ch04.open.tension: Is the Hubble tension a sign of unrecognised errors in the measurements, or of new physics?
ch04.open.darkEnergy: What is dark energy, and does it change over time?
ch04.caption.galaxies: Across the universe, galaxies gather in countless numbers.
ch04.caption.stretch: Space itself grows, and carries the galaxies apart.
ch04.caption.redshift: Light from distant galaxies arrives stretched toward the red.
ch04.caption.tension: Two ways of measuring the expansion disagree, and no one yet knows why.
ch04.caption.sideBySide: The verse and the science are placed side by side for reflection, not as proof of one another.
ch05.intro.title: Seven heavens and the galaxies
ch05.intro.subtitle: From our own galaxy to the edge of what we can see
ch05.scholarly.classical.seven: The Quran affirms seven heavens. Most classical scholars understood them as real realms, largely beyond what we can observe.
ch05.scholarly.modern.notIdentified: Some modern writers have tried to match the seven heavens with layers of the atmosphere or with structures in the cosmos. Such matchings are modern and are not made here: this scene shows only observable structure and does not identify the seven heavens with it.
ch05.science.galaxies: Galaxies grew where gas fell into the knots of the dark-matter web, cooled and formed stars. Ours, the Milky Way, is a barred spiral galaxy. It is shown here as an artist’s model, since we cannot see it from outside.
ch05.science.sdss: Every other point of light here is a real galaxy at its measured position: {count} galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey’s twentieth data release, out to redshift {z}, whose light set out up to {lookback} billion years ago.
ch05.science.web: Together they trace the cosmic web: walls and filaments of galaxies around vast, emptier voids. The survey’s shape comes from where its telescope could look, mostly away from the dusty plane of our own galaxy. Later the view brightens one slice along the celestial equator, about 160 million light-years thick. The long arc of galaxies across it is the Sloan Great Wall, found in this survey’s maps.
ch05.science.observable: The observable universe is far larger still. Its radius today is about {radius} billion light-years, larger than the light-travel time alone suggests, because space kept expanding while the oldest light was on its way.
ch05.open.darkMatter: Most of the matter shaping this web is dark matter. What it is remains unknown.
ch05.open.beyond: Does the universe beyond our horizon look like the part we can see? It cannot be observed, so for now no one can say.
ch05.caption.milkyWay: Our home galaxy, the Milky Way, shown as an artist’s model.
ch05.caption.pullBack: Drawing back, our galaxy becomes one point of light among many.
ch05.caption.survey: Each point of light now is a real galaxy, mapped by the Sloan Digital Sky Survey.
ch05.caption.observable: Everything we can observe lies within the distance light has travelled since the beginning.
ch06.intro.title: Stars and iron
ch06.intro.subtitle: How stars forge the elements, and scatter them
ch06.note.cattle: Shown for comparison: here the same verb, anzala (“sent down”), is used of livestock.
ch06.scholarly.classical.might: Ibn Kathir explains the “great might” (ba’s shadid) of iron as weapons of war, a deterrent against those who reject the truth once it has been made clear, and its benefits for people as the tools of daily life: for crafts, for farming and for the home.
ch06.scholarly.classical.anzalna: Al-Qurtubi records that “We sent down” (anzalna) is read by some, among them al-Hasan, as “We brought into being”, just as livestock are said to be “sent down” in 39:6. Ibn Zayd and others read it as Allah (glorified and exalted is He) bringing iron out of the earth and teaching people to work it.
ch06.scholarly.modern.space: Some modern writers read anzalna al-hadid as iron arriving from space, in meteorites or from exploding stars. This is a modern reading, and it is debated.
ch06.science.onion: Massive stars fuse ever heavier elements in nested shells: hydrogen, helium, carbon, oxygen and silicon. Fusion stops at the “iron peak”: beyond it, fusing nuclei releases no more energy.
ch06.science.nickel: Silicon burning makes nickel-56, which decays through cobalt-56 into stable iron-56, with half-lives of {ni} and {co} days.
ch06.science.collapse: When the iron core of a massive star can no longer hold itself up, it collapses in a fraction of a second. A shock wave and a burst of neutrinos then blow the star apart in a core-collapse supernova, scattering the elements it made into space.
ch06.science.typeIa: A white dwarf in a close pair of stars can also explode, as a Type Ia supernova. By recent estimates, these thermonuclear explosions made about half of the universe’s iron, and core-collapse supernovae most of the rest.
ch06.science.us: Much of the iron on Earth, including the iron in our blood, was made in such stars.
ch06.open.mechanism: Exactly how the shock wave of a core-collapse supernova is revived to blow the star apart is still being worked out.
ch06.open.progenitors: Which kinds of star systems explode as Type Ia supernovae is still debated.
ch06.caption.star: A massive star burns heavier and heavier elements, layer upon layer.
ch06.caption.iron: At its heart, fusion reaches iron, and can go no further.
ch06.caption.collapse: The core collapses; a shock wave and a flood of neutrinos tear the star apart.
ch06.caption.elements: Its debris carries the elements it made out into space.
ch06.caption.whiteDwarf: Elsewhere, a white dwarf draws gas from a companion star.
ch06.caption.typeIa: It explodes as a Type Ia supernova, forging much of the universe’s iron.
ch06.caption.us: Much of the iron on Earth, and in our blood, was made in such stars.
